title: Monitoring training intensity
log: 2026-10-29T12:14:26Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

draft.title: Monitoring training intensity
card: Intensity is shown as a percentage of maximum heart rate (MHR). A common estimate is MHR = 220 minus age. A 17-year-old's estimated MHR is about 203 beats per minute.
The rating of perceived exertion is the person's own score for how hard the effort feels, on a scale such as 6 to 20 or 0 to 10. A higher score means harder effort.
At lower intensity a person can talk in full sentences. At moderate intensity speech becomes broken. At high intensity they can say only a word or two.
Heart rate zones use a measured number. RPE and the talk test rely on how the person feels, so they need no equipment.
draft.remember: Intensity can be tracked by heart rate, by how hard it feels, or by how well you can talk.

a.q: During a run, Jo can speak only one or two words at a time before she must breathe. Which method is she using, and what does it suggest?
opts: Heart rate zones, suggesting low intensity
a.why: Judging effort by how much she can say is the talk test. Only a word or two at a time points to high intensity. Low intensity would let her speak in full sentences.
a.clue: Which method is based on how well she can speak?

b.q: Sam, aged 16, has no heart rate monitor. He wants to check his effort during a swim set. Which method suits him, and why?
opts: RPE, as it needs only his own score of effort
Heart rate zones, as they need only his age
RPE, as it gives a measured percentage of MHR
Talk test, as it gives an exact heart rate
b.why: RPE relies on how hard the effort feels to Sam, so it needs no equipment. Heart rate zones are tied to a measured heart rate, so a monitor or a pulse count is needed to use them. RPE does not give a percentage of MHR.
b.clue: Which method relies on how the effort feels?

b.best: RPE, as it needs only his own score of effort
